The words

Though lonely be thy path, fear not, for He
Who marks the sparrow fall is guarding thee;
And not a star shines o'er thy head by night,
But He hath known that it will reach thy sight.

And not a grief can darken or surprise,
Swell in thy heart, or dim with tears thine eyes,
But it is sent in mercy and in love,
To bid thy helplessness seek strength above.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum F and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (C).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

These words were printed without an author's name in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1848), as hymn 336, “The Strength of the Lonely”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Tens (10.10.10.10) (10.10.10.10), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to SONG TWENTY-TWO; any other Tens (10.10.10.10) tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Anonymous
  • Music (1623): Orlando Gibbons (1583–1625)

Questions about Though Lonely Be Thy Path, Fear Not, for He

What is the doh of Though Lonely Be Thy Path, Fear Not, for He?

In this version, in F major, doh is F. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Though Lonely Be Thy Path, Fear Not, for He start on?

It starts on s (C in F major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is Though Lonely Be Thy Path, Fear Not, for He in the public domain?

Yes. Orlando Gibbons died in 1625; the words were in print by 1848 and the music in 1623. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
